content.overview: The tribunal may rule on its own jurisdiction. The arbitration clause is separable from the host contract.
content.study: Raise the objection by the statement of defence. A section 16 dismissal of the objection is usually taken in the final award and then in section 34. Do not run a parallel civil suit on the same jurisdictional quarrel.

learningObjectives: State the rule recorded for Section 16 Arbitration Act — Kompetenz-kompetenz.
Separate the points already present in the topic sections.
Do not add a case or section number that is not already in this note.
enhancement.definition: Section 16 embodies the tribunal's competence-competence and separability principles: the arbitral tribunal may rule on its own jurisdiction, including objections to the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement, and an arbitration clause is treated as an agreement independent of the other contract terms for the statutory purpose.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Jurisdictional objections are primarily addressed within the arbitral process under Section 16. The arbitration clause's separability means that an allegation that the main contract is void does not by itself eliminate the tribunal's authority to consider the arbitration agreement.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 — Section 16 Arbitration Act — Kompetenz-kompetenz
essentialIngredients: An arbitral tribunal has been constituted.
A jurisdictional objection falls within Section 16.
The objection is raised in accordance with the statutory timing framework.
The tribunal determines the jurisdictional issue within the Act's competence-competence and separability framework.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 16 covers objections that the tribunal lacks jurisdiction and objections exceeding the scope of its authority. A plea that the arbitration agreement is invalid is distinct from a plea concerning the underlying contract. Section 16 also prescribes when jurisdictional objections should be raised and provides for the statutory consequences following the tribunal's ruling.

examples.title: Challenge to tribunal jurisdiction
examples.body: A respondent contends that the dispute falls outside the arbitration clause. The respondent should frame the objection under Section 16 and identify whether it concerns the tribunal's jurisdiction or excess of authority.

examples.title: Main contract alleged void
examples.body: A party alleges that the main contract is void. The analysis must separately consider the arbitration agreement because the statutory separability principle prevents the validity of the main contract from automatically answering the arbitration-clause question.

enhancement.problemApplication: A respondent argues that the main contract is void and therefore the arbitral tribunal has no jurisdiction. Apply Section 16 by separating the validity of the underlying contract from the arbitration agreement and identifying the tribunal's statutory power to rule on its own jurisdiction.
keyTakeaways: The arbitration clause is treated separately from the main contract.
Jurisdictional objections have statutory timing requirements.
Section 16 should not be confused with a general merits defence.

notes: Enhancement expanded from migrated baseline using the current statutory structure identified in India Code. Independent legal verification remains a separate gate.

distinctions: Jurisdiction objection vs merits objection: the former concerns the tribunal's authority; the latter concerns the substantive dispute.
Separability vs invalidity of main contract: invalidity of the main contract does not automatically invalidate the arbitration agreement.
enhancement.examAnswerStructure: For 10 marks: competence-competence → separability → types of jurisdictional objection → timing → application. For 16 marks add scope-of-authority objections, procedural consequences, and relationship with Sections 8, 11 and 34.
